Each run's code-review-input.ex equals evals/cases/code-review-input.ex. Every assistant message carries the run's own model; `claude-fable-5-1` appears only as `advisorModel` metadata and in environment text. Both haiku runs made one advisor call (server_tool_use `advisor`, result encrypted) before writing review.md, so their output may carry advice from that model; the sonnet runs made none.

All four read SKILL.md, ecto-phoenix.md and processes.md before writing review.md (sonnet-1 and sonnet-2 with `cat`). Haiku-1 only parsed its blocks with `elixir -e`. Haiku-2 copied both blocks to skill-haiku-2/tmp-check/, ran `mix format --check-formatted` (the schema failed on `field` parentheses, which its line 152 explains), and its `rm` of the folder was refused, so tmp-check/ remains in the run folder; both files there match its review blocks byte for byte. Sonnet-1 ran `which elixir` but never formatted and says on line 3 that Elixir was not run. Sonnet-2's format attempts needed approval and it says so in its reply. No result.json carries format_ok, so format_ok comes from this grade's own check.

Rule list: the same 16 index rows as 2026-10-31-b. `git diff 74112b4 -- idiomatic-elixir/` (working tree) changes three of them. 'Match every expected shape...' now states the different-reasons sentence the earlier grades applied by convention ("Different failures need different reasons too: a caller cannot tell a missing field from a bad number when both return `{:error, :invalid}`.") and adds the `==` sentence; the identical-errors verdicts rest on the first. 'Use `and`, `or`, `not`...' adds "and for operands that can be `nil`, such as `opts[:verbose]`, which `and` and `not` raise on"; that sentence now says outright that input line 27 is correct, and sonnet-1 (finding 10, line 25) and sonnet-2 (finding 9, line 23) still put line 27 under the operator rule. Both also report line 21 and their code has no `&&`, so the verdict stays clean by the earlier convention and the false positive is recorded under the must-not-report check. 'Return `{:ok, value}`...' adds the nil-for-absence sentence, which no output exercises. 'Validate input with changesets' changes only the accessor sentence (`changed?/3`), which no output exercises. Outside the list, the `->` rule was rewritten; see below.

Planted problems are mapped as in 2026-10-31-b: 21 problems from the case table's rows, with the line 15-17 rebinding counted apart from the magic 120 and the line 49 spawn apart from the closure copy. A problem counts as reported only when a finding names it or its stated fix addresses it; a silent fix does not count, and a rule is violated when a planted problem belonging to it goes unreported. Counts: haiku-1 18/21 (missing both magic numbers and the dead `is_binary`); haiku-2 20/21 (missing the magic 18); sonnet-1 17/21 (missing the nesting, both magic numbers and the dead `is_binary`); sonnet-2 18/21 (missing the line 8 raise outside the `try` and both magic numbers). All four report the line 24 lookup-before-insert with the race and replace it with `unique_constraint(:email)` in a companion changeset.

Judgment calls. Sonnet-1's line 8 raise counts through finding 1 (line 7, "It also raises on a missing role (`nil`)."), as 2026-10-31-b counted sonnet-1's "a missing role raises". Sonnet-2's does not: finding 1 names only atom exhaustion, finding 2 the rescue and finding 6 only input lines 12-13, and its `validate_required` covers a missing role only silently, so 'Return {:ok, value}...' is violated for sonnet-2 and for the Sonnet tier. Haiku-2's magic 120 counts through finding 2's `@max_age`; its 18 is in no finding, and `@min_age 18` (line 110) is a silent fix, which by the standard still leaves 'Comments explain why...' violated. Haiku-1 is violated on that rule three ways: no finding names either number, its schema keeps both literals (lines 117-118), and line 116 drops the line 11 why-comment that its finding 18 says stays. Sonnet-1 and sonnet-2 now name the closure copy (findings 11 and 13) but keep `user` captured in the closure, so 'Send processes only the data they need' is violated by the code itself and the applies-every-finding check is missed. Haiku-2's private `maybe_send_welcome/2` returns `{:ok, pid}` from line 85 and `:ok` from line 86; earlier grades judged 'Give each function one return shape' on the public function only and passed one-armed `if ..., do: send_welcome(user)` with the same mixed value, so this is kept clean for comparability and not counted.

Sonnet-1 line 67, `put_change(changeset, :nickname, get_field(changeset, :nickname) || get_field(changeset, :email))`, is 99 columns at the snippet's own indentation and `mix format` spreads it over five lines. 'Name a step instead of wrapping an expression' is decided by its first sentences, "When `mix format` spreads an expression over several lines, the expression is as hard to read as before; what helps is finding the distinct conceptual steps inside it and giving one a name, when the name says something." The default nickname is such a step (haiku-2 names it `nickname`, line 141), so the rule is violated. This is a new Sonnet reading compared with 2026-10-31-b, whose Sonnet code passed the format check. The same line is listed under 'Before you finish' step 1, since the run had Elixir available and did not format.

The `->` rule, "Put each `->` body on its own line unless the clauses read as a table", is not in this case's list, so its breaks go to other_violations, graded against the rewritten text. Haiku-1 lines 125-126 (`nil -> put_change(...)` beside `_nickname -> changeset`, 69 columns after indentation) break under "A row that calls on, as `{:ok, bytes} -> hash_if_canonical(token, bytes)` does beside `_other -> :error`, does not read that way, because one row gives an answer and the other hands off"; the earlier text, which allowed a body "simple enough to take in together with its pattern", would have let it stand. Haiku-2 lines 91-93 put a one-expression `fn` body below the head although the call takes 89 columns on one line, which breaks "A single-clause `fn` passed as an argument follows the one-expression rule instead: one expression stays on the `fn`'s line, more goes below." The sonnet `fn`s would take 103 columns on one line, so they stay broken, as 2026-10-31-b ruled. Sonnet-2's `case` at lines 117-123 puts each body below.

One-line `if ..., do: ..., else: ...`: none in any improved code block. Haiku-1 and haiku-2 keep the cap. None of these changes a verdict.
